To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ceramide glucosyl‐ and galactosyl‐transferases are differentially regulated during development of the cerebellum and that these enzymes can be modulated by agents that inhibit myelination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of myelin formation in vitro, and with the possible role of CGalT as a marker of myelinogenesis.
the development of a model system for the study of myelinogenesis in vitro.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

BUdR inhibits myelination in vitro and that the mechanism of the inhibition is not yet known, and that EAE serum inhibits myelinating activity in vitro but the mechanism of the inhibitory activity is not known.
the CGalT and CGlcT activities in the cultures are not identical with those in vivo and that BUdR and EAE serum inhibit myelination by different mechanisms.

the inhibition of myelin formation by BUdR is due to the inhibition of the synthesis of myelin‐forming cells and that this inhibition is not mediated by inhibition of myelin‐specific glycosyltransferases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inhibition of myelination by BUdR or by EAE serum is associated with a reduction of the glial enzyme CGalT.
the inhibition of myelination by BUdR, by EAE serum and by EAE‐induced demyelination in vivo may be due in part to a reduction in CGalT activity in glial cells.
CGalT activity was reduced by 22% and 28% by BUdR (inhibition of myelination) and EAE serum (demyelination), respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ceramide galactoside synthetase activity is predominantly glial and that this enzyme is reduced in demyelination.
we can use these enzymes to study demyelination and remyelination in vitro, in a system that can be manipulated in many ways.

we have shown that the activity of CGalT is reduced by 50% in the presence of BUdR and that the activity of the enzyme is reduced by about 50% in cultures maintained in the presence of serum from EAE‐induced rabbits.
